Look into the night sky.
On a clear night,
away from city lights,
you can see a
few thousand stars.
Our galaxy holds hundreds
of billions of them,
and many are billions
of years older than our Sun.
According to the Kardashev
scale, a civilization that
keeps growing keeps using
more energy.
Some estimates suggest
that a civilization
expanding across a galaxy
could do it in
a few million to
a few tens of
millions of years.
That is a blink
in cosmic time,
and our galaxy is
billions of years old,
so there has been
more than enough of it.
So why is the
cosmos so quiet?
Why have our radio
telescopes found no
confirmed signal from anyone
else?
This puzzle is known
as the Fermi paradox.
One proposed answer is
the Great Filter,
an idea from economist
Robin Hanson.
Somewhere on the path
from lifeless matter to
a galaxy-spanning
civilization, there may
be a step that
almost nobody survives.
One version of the
idea suspects the step
is the jump from
Type Zero to Type One.
A species that learns
to command planetary energy
may gain the power
to destroy itself before
it learns to cooperate.
Think about our own world.
Within about seven years
of the discovery of
nuclear fission, the first
atomic bombs existed.
We burned fossil fuels
to drive global industry,
and that is now
changing the climate.
We are building artificial
intelligence and
biotechnology with global
consequences, while our
institutions are still
learning how to manage
global risks.
Reaching Type One may
mean surviving our own
technological childhood.
If the silence of
space tells us anything,
it might be that
many civilizations stumble
during this exact phase.
But nobody knows.
The silence has other
possible explanations,
and the Great Filter
is only a hypothesis.
Humanity sits near Type
zero point seven,
balanced on the edge
of that razor.
Will we reach the
stars, or will we
join the silence?

of humanity's cosmic ranking
and our path forward
